What is the difference between a fact and an opinion?
Name three things a person needs to survive.
What do you already know about the Amazon rainforest?

teach.heading: Retrieval and inference
bullets: Retrieval: the text tells you directly
Inference: you read between the lines
Both need evidence from the text
teach.note: Read Chapters 1–2 aloud from the class copy (pupils follow in theirs). Pause after the crash and ask for one fact and one inference. Misconception: pupils treat any sentence about the book as an inference; push for 'which words make you think that?'

left.title: Retrieval
points: The answer is on the page

right.title: Inference
points: What sort of person is he?

teach.heading: How openings hook us
bullets: Start in the middle of the action
Create questions in the reader's mind
Give us someone to care about
teach.note: Ask: 'What questions does the opening make you ask?' Collect three in the chat. Link to the big question: one event (the crash) changes everything.

teach.heading: Practise on a short extract
bullets: Read the teacher-written extract
Retrieve, then infer
teach.note: Use this original extract to model, so we are not quoting the novel. Ask: what can we retrieve? What can we infer about the speaker?

quote.text: The engine coughed twice, then fell silent. Through the window, the green went on forever, and Sami realised he could no longer hear his own heartbeat over the roaring wind.

teach.heading: Writing an inference
bullets: Point, then evidence, then explain
teach.note: Model on the shared screen.

model.problem: What can we infer about Sami from the extract?
steps: Point: Sami is terrified
Evidence: he 'could no longer hear his own heartbeat over the roaring wind'
Explain: the noise overwhelms him, suggesting panic and danger
model.answer: A short inference paragraph using evidence

teach.heading: Check: retrieve or infer?
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: 'The engine coughed twice, then fell silent.' Which is an INFERENCE?
check.why: The danger is suggested, not stated. A, B and D are stated or retrieved.

practice: Retrieve two facts about the plane journey from Chapter 1.
Write one inference about Fred with a piece of evidence.
List two questions the opening makes you ask.
independent: Core: Write a PEE paragraph: What is your first impression of Fred?
Extend: Explain how the writer hooks the reader in the opening, using two pieces of evidence.
Stretch: Predict how Fred might change by the end of the novel. Justify your prediction with clues from Chapters 1–2.
exit: What is the difference between retrieval and inference?
Write one inference about the setting.
Make one prediction with a reason.
lessons.homework: Read Chapters 3–4 and record two facts and two inferences in your reading journal.
lessons.send: Support: sentence starters ('I can infer that… because…') and the audio version of the chapters. EAL: key word cards. Stretch: compare with another survival story you know.

teach.heading: VANCAPPI: our word-class toolkit
teach.note: Display the school's VANCAPPI poster. Pupils hold up one example for each on the mini-whiteboard.

teach.heading: Sentence boundaries
teach.note: Two complete sentences need a full stop, a semi-colon or a conjunction between them, never just a comma.

misconception.wrong: The plane fell, the children screamed.
misconception.right: The plane fell. The children screamed. / The plane fell and the children screamed.

teach.heading: Model: fix and upgrade
teach.note: Think aloud through the steps.

model.problem: Fix: 'Con was scared she walked slowly through the trees'
steps: Find the two main clauses: Con was scared | she walked slowly...
Choose a boundary: full stop or conjunction
Upgrade the verb: walked becomes edged
Check: capital letter and full stop
model.answer: Con was scared, so she edged slowly through the trees.

teach.heading: Hinge: which is correct?
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
options: The river was fast, Max held on.
The river was fast. Max held on.
The river was fast Max held on.
check.why: Only B separates the two main clauses; A is a comma splice and C is a run-on sentence.

practice.q: Label every word in: 'Suddenly, the small boat drifted beneath the dark trees.'
practice.a: Suddenly (adverb), the (determiner), small (adjective), boat (noun), drifted (verb), beneath (preposition), the (determiner), dark (adjective), trees (noun).
practice.model: Work left to right: ask 'what job does this word do?' Suddenly tells when (adverb). Small describes boat (adjective). Boat is a thing (noun). Drifted is the action (verb). Beneath shows position (preposition). Note 'the' is a determiner, a word class beyond VANCAPPI.

practice.q: Fix the comma splice: 'Lila found water, she shared it with everyone.'
practice.a: Lila found water. She shared it with everyone. (or: Lila found water and she shared it with everyone.)

independent.q: Core: correct the five sentence-boundary errors in the paragraph on the pupil PDF.
independent.a: Each comma splice or run-on is split with a full stop or joined with a conjunction (and, but, so, because).
independent.model: First error: 'The rain stopped, the forest steamed.' Two main clauses, so: 'The rain stopped. The forest steamed.' or 'The rain stopped and the forest steamed.'

independent.q: Extend: write three sentences about surviving in the rainforest, each using a different conjunction.
independent.a: For example: Fred climbed the tree because he wanted to see the river.

independent.q: Stretch: write one sentence containing all eight VANCAPPI word classes.
independent.a: For example: 'Oh, she quickly ran under the bridge and hid.' (interjection Oh, pronoun she, adverb quickly, verb ran, preposition under, noun bridge, conjunction and, verb hid; add an adjective: 'the old bridge').

exit.q: Which word class is 'although'?
Write the shortest sentence you can with a verb, a noun and an interjection.

lessons.homework: Grammar Booklet: VANCAPPI and sentence boundaries exercises; learn the eight word classes in order.
lessons.send: SEND: VANCAPPI card with colour-coded examples. EAL: bilingual word-class glossary. Stretch: identify determiners and modal verbs as well.

Tangled roots on a rainforest floor

resources: Tarbiyyah Secondary English scheme of work 2026-27, Year 7 HT1 weekly scheme (The Explorer: setting and language analysis)
Teacher-written rainforest setting extract (on the slides and pupil PDF)
Reading Journal (school template)
Pupil PDF worksheet (printable or for a drawing tablet)

starter.q: Which sentence uses a full stop correctly?
options: The river was wide. It was brown.
The river was wide it was brown.
starter.a: A) The river was wide. It was brown.

options: a fact copied from the text
an idea worked out from clues
starter.a: B) an idea worked out from clues

teach.heading: The Explorer: what we need to know
bullets: Four children survive a plane crash in the Amazon.
The rainforest is both beautiful and deadly.
The novel asks: how do people change through hardship?
teach.note: Introduce Katherine Rundell's novel (2017) as the school's Year 7 Autumn text. Pupils will read it in full in Autumn 2027; today we learn the skill of reading a setting. Show the map picture and ask what pupils already know about the Amazon.

teach.heading: Words that build a setting
bullets: Precise nouns: canopy, vines, roots
Powerful verbs: dripped, coiled, swallowed
Adjectives that carry mood: humid, tangled, silent
teach.note: Use this teacher-written line: 'The trees swallowed the light, and the air hung heavy and wet.' Ask which word does the most work. Draw out 'swallowed' (personification: the forest seems alive and hungry).

quote.text: The trees swallowed the light, and the air hung heavy and wet. Somewhere above, something shrieked and fell silent.

teach.heading: Model: from word to effect
teach.note: Think aloud. Show how one word leads to an inference about the place and the character.

model.problem: What does 'swallowed' suggest about the rainforest?
steps: Find the word: swallowed
Literal meaning: eaten whole
Connotation: hunger, danger, being trapped
Inference: the forest feels alive and threatening
model.answer: The verb 'swallowed' makes the forest seem like a hungry creature, so the reader senses danger.

teach.heading: Hinge: which word builds tension?
teach.note: Poll. Reveal the answer and discuss why the others are weaker.

check.q: Which word makes the setting most threatening?
check.why: 'Shrieked' is a sudden, frightening sound; 'green' and 'trees' are neutral, 'wet' is uncomfortable but not threatening.

practice.q: Explain what 'hung heavy' suggests about the air.
practice.a: It suggests the air is thick, humid and hard to breathe, creating an oppressive mood.
practice.model: Word: hung heavy. Meaning: the air feels weighed down. Connotation: pressure, discomfort. Inference: the heat is oppressive and the place feels hostile.

practice.q: Find a word in the extract that shows sound and explain its effect.
practice.a: 'Shrieked': a sudden scream that breaks the silence and makes the reader jump.

independent.q: Core: write three sentences explaining how the extract makes the rainforest feel dangerous. Use 'This suggests...' in each.
independent.a: For example: The verb 'swallowed' suggests the forest is alive and hungry. This suggests the children could be trapped...
independent.model: The verb 'swallowed' suggests the trees are like a hungry animal. This suggests the rainforest could trap anyone inside it. The reader feels uneasy because the place itself seems alive.

independent.q: Extend: add a sentence about how a lost child might feel in this setting.
independent.a: For example: A lost child would feel small and watched, because the forest seems to have a will of its own.

independent.q: Stretch: write your own sentence about the rainforest using one verb that makes it seem alive.
independent.a: For example: Vines coiled around the trunks like patient snakes.

exit.q: Which is the best explanation?
options: 'Swallowed' makes the forest seem hungry and alive
exit.a: B) 'Swallowed' makes the forest seem hungry and alive

exit.q: Return to the ponder question: which word from today would you use to describe that first sound, and why?
exit.a: Answers vary, e.g. 'shrieked', because it is sudden and frightening.

lessons.homework: Read the setting extract on the pupil PDF again and underline five words that build atmosphere; start your Reading Journal with the date and one new word.
lessons.send: SEND: word bank with meanings and a 'This suggests...' sentence starter. EAL: picture glossary of rainforest nouns. Stretch: comment on how two words work together.

Green pen for DIRT

starter.q: Where does the comma go? 'When night fell the house creaked.'
What does PETZAAL's E stand for?

teach.heading: STASS: the school's setting framework
teach.note: Go through each letter with an example from the old house.

head: Step
Ask
Example
rows: Bruised clouds pressed down on the roof.
It was the hour after sunset.
The silence felt like held breath.
From the gate, up the path, to the door.

teach.heading: Model: a STASS paragraph
teach.note: Read the model and label each step together.

model.problem: Describe an old house at dusk
steps: Sky: Bruised clouds pressed down on the slate roof.
Time: It was the hour when shadows grow long.
Atmosphere: As I stepped closer, the silence felt like held breath.
Significant object: Inside, a clock had stopped at 3:17.
Spatial order: From the gate to the door, weeds swallowed the path.
model.answer: A paragraph where the weather, time and objects build one mood.

teach.heading: Hinge
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: 'Rain wept against the window as she waited alone.' This is...
check.why: The weather (weeping rain) mirrors a sad, lonely feeling: pathetic fallacy.

practice.q: Plan your STASS grid for 'a corridor in an old school at night'.
practice.a: Five notes, one per STASS step.
practice.model: Sky: wind moaning at the windows. Time: midnight. Atmosphere: watchful, still. Significant object: a single locker door swinging. Spatial order: from the stairs, along the corridor, to the last classroom.

practice.q: Write your Sky sentence using pathetic fallacy.
practice.a: For example: Outside, the wind moaned as if it had lost something.

independent.q: Core: write your STASS setting paragraph in the portal response box (at least six sentences, one complex sentence). Starter: 'Outside, the wind...'
independent.a: A paragraph using all five STASS steps, a complex sentence and precise verbs.
independent.model: Outside, the wind moaned against the tall windows. It was midnight, and the school had forgotten its daytime noise. As I walked along the corridor, my footsteps sounded too loud. Halfway down, a single locker door swung open and shut. At the far end, the last classroom glowed with a pale light that should not have been there.

independent.q: DIRT: use the feedback code to improve two sentences in green pen.
independent.a: Two sentences improved (verb, boundary or clause).

independent.q: Stretch: change the mood of one sentence from creepy to peaceful by changing only two words.
independent.a: For example: 'the wind moaned' becomes 'the wind whispered'; 'should not' becomes 'seemed to'.

exit.q: What does the first S in STASS stand for?
Return to the ponder: which words changed the mood most, and why?
exit.a: Usually the verbs and the weather, because they carry feelings.

lessons.homework: Write a STASS paragraph about your street at dawn; label each step.
lessons.send: SEND: STASS planning grid with word bank. EAL: model paragraph to adapt by changing nouns. Stretch: use pathetic fallacy and a relative clause.

Which continent is the Amazon rainforest in?

teach.heading: Features of an information text
bullets: Title and headings
Topic sentences
Facts and figures
Formal, third-person voice
teach.note: Show the teacher-written text on the pupil PDF: 'The Amazon Rainforest'. Ask pupils to spot each feature before you name it.

teach.heading: The rainforest in layers
teach.note: Teach the four layers from the diagram picture; this is the information pupils will retrieve.

items: Forest floor: roots and fallen leaves

teach.heading: Model: retrieve, then summarise
teach.note: Show how to find facts quickly by scanning for key words, then squeeze a paragraph into one sentence.

model.problem: Summarise the paragraph on the canopy.
steps: Scan for the heading 'The canopy'
Underline the topic sentence
Pick two key facts
Write one sentence in your own words
model.answer: The canopy is a thick roof of leaves where most rainforest animals live.

teach.heading: Hinge: what is a topic sentence for?
teach.note: Poll, then discuss.

check.q: A topic sentence...
options: tells the reader what the paragraph is about
check.why: It introduces the paragraph's main idea; it is not the end, and it is rarely a question.

practice.q: Retrieve two facts about the forest floor from the text.
practice.a: It is dark because little sunlight reaches it; it is covered in roots and fallen leaves.
practice.model: Scan for 'forest floor'. Read the topic sentence. Copy the two facts in short phrases: dark, little sunlight; roots and fallen leaves.

practice.q: Which heading would you look under to find out about jaguars?
practice.a: The understorey or forest floor section, where large animals hunt.

independent.q: Core: answer the four retrieval questions on the pupil PDF in full sentences.
independent.a: Answers from the teacher-written text: the four layers, the canopy roof, the dark understorey, the forest floor's roots and leaves.
independent.model: Question: Why is the understorey dark? Answer in a full sentence using the question's words: The understorey is dark because the canopy above blocks most of the sunlight.

independent.q: Extend: summarise the whole text in two sentences.
independent.a: For example: The Amazon is the largest tropical rainforest, arranged in layers from the emergent trees to the forest floor. Each layer has its own conditions and wildlife.

independent.q: Stretch: how would Fred, Con, Lila and Max use this information to survive? Give one idea.
independent.a: For example: they could look for food and water near the river, because the forest floor is dark and hard to search.

exit.q: Which is a summary?
Is 'the lungs of the Earth' a fair name? Give one reason from today.
exit.a: Answers vary, e.g. yes, because its vast canopy of trees takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen.

lessons.homework: Find one fact about an Amazon animal and write it as a topic sentence plus two supporting facts.
lessons.send: SEND: retrieval questions with paragraph numbers. EAL: key word glossary with pictures. Stretch: explain why the text uses the third person.

quote.text:
William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564, the son of a glove-maker. At eighteen he married, and by his late twenties he was in London, writing and acting.

In 1599 his company opened the Globe, an open-air theatre on the south bank of the Thames. There, and later at the indoor Blackfriars, his plays drew crowds of every class.

When James I became king in 1603, the company became the King's Men. The Tempest, one of the last plays he wrote alone, was performed at court in 1611.

Shakespeare died in 1616. Seven years later, two friends collected his plays in the First Folio. Without their loyalty, half his plays might have been lost for ever.
quote.source: 'The Man Behind the Plays', a teacher-written biography for TGA

teach.heading: The discussion (teacher-written)
teach.note: Read aloud; pupils highlight 'for' in one colour and 'against' in another.

quote.text:
Forgiveness is often praised, but is it always right? Supporters argue that forgiving frees the victim: resentment, they say, is a weight that only the forgiver can put down. Families and friendships survive because people pardon each other's mistakes.

Yet others warn that forgiving too quickly can excuse wrongdoing. If an offender is not sorry, forgiveness may simply invite the harm again. Justice, they insist, must come first.

Perhaps the answer lies between the two: forgiveness is strongest when the truth is faced and the wrong is put right.
quote.source: 'The Hardest Word', a teacher-written discussion article for TGA

teach.note: Sort the arguments.

teach.heading: The review (teacher-written)
teach.note: Read aloud. Pupils mark S for summary and E for evaluation in the margin.

quote.text:
The Tempest begins with a shipwreck and ends with a pardon. In between, an exiled duke gathers his enemies on a magic island and must decide what to do with them.

It is the ending that makes the play extraordinary. Prospero could destroy those who ruined him; instead he forgives them. Shakespeare gives him a line that still feels brave: 'The rarer action is / In virtue than in vengeance.'

Not every thread is tied. Antonio barely speaks, and Caliban's future is uncertain. Yet this honesty is a strength: forgiveness here is a choice, not a fairy tale. Four centuries on, it remains a play worth arguing about.
quote.source: 'A Storm, Then Peace', a teacher-written review for TGA

practice.q: How does the reviewer turn a weakness into a strength?
practice.a: Untied threads are called 'honesty': forgiveness is shown as a real choice, not a fairy tale.

independent.a: Answers vary with a reason.

exit.a: I trust a review that gives evidence and admits weaknesses as well as strengths.

model.problem: Is Prospero a hero or a tyrant?
steps: Interpretation 1: a hero who chooses 'virtue' over 'vengeance'
Interpretation 2: a tyrant who keeps Ariel and Caliban as servants
Weigh: his final choices free Ariel and pardon his enemies

practice.q: Embed: rewrite 'Ariel says All hail, great master. This shows obedience.'
practice.a: Ariel greets Prospero with 'All hail, great master!', which shows his eager obedience.

independent.q: Extend: how might an actor show the 'controller' reading on stage?

independent.q: Stretch: why do great plays allow more than one interpretation?
independent.a: Because characters are complex, like real people, so readers debate them.

teach.heading: Hinge: what the metaphor suggests

check.q: Why might Zephaniah write about Britain as a recipe?
options: to say one group is more important
to show many peoples mixed over time make one whole
to give instructions for cooking dinner
check.why: A recipe needs every ingredient, mixed with care; the poem says Britain is made the same way.

teach.heading: Model: the final instruction
teach.note: I do. Read the last two lines aloud, then build the paragraph live.

model.problem: How does Zephaniah present Britain in the ending?
steps: Point: Zephaniah ends by showing how Britain should be treated
Evidence: 'Serve with justice / And enjoy.'
Technique: imperative verbs, the end of the recipe
Zoom in: 'justice' is an unusual thing to serve; it means fairness
Link: a country of many peoples only works if it is fair
model.answer: Zephaniah ends with the imperatives 'Serve with justice / And enjoy', so the recipe becomes a rule for living: Britain is only complete when every ingredient is treated fairly.

practice.q: Model with me: write a PETZAAL Point and Evidence on the recipe metaphor
practice.a: For example: Zephaniah presents Britain as a dish made over centuries; 'Take some Picts, Celts and Silures' starts the recipe in ancient history.
practice.model: Point: Zephaniah presents Britain as something made, like a meal. | Evidence: 'Take some Picts, Celts and Silures' | Technique: imperative verb 'Take', the language of recipes | Zoom in: 'Take' tells us to begin with Britain's oldest peoples | Analyse: the country was built step by step | Alternative: some readers may see it as playful, not serious | Link: Britain belongs to all its ingredients.

practice.q: Find one more recipe verb in the poem and say what it suggests
practice.a: For example: 'add' suggests each new people joins rather than replaces

independent.q: Core: in the portal response box, write a full PETZAAL paragraph: 'How does Zephaniah present Britain as a place where many cultures belong?' Starter: 'Zephaniah presents Britain as...'
independent.a: A PETZAAL paragraph using the recipe metaphor and the ending, with an embedded quotation.
independent.model: Point: Zephaniah presents Britain as a mixture where every culture belongs. | Evidence: 'Serve with justice' | Technique: extended metaphor and imperative | Zoom in: 'justice' | Analyse: fairness is the final ingredient that holds the mixture together | Alternative: the humour may make a serious point easier to hear | Link: belonging is something a country must serve to everyone.

independent.q: Extend: in your Reading Journal, explain why the order of the ingredients matters
independent.a: It follows history: early Britons, Romans, Saxons, Vikings, Normans, then modern arrivals, so Britain has always been mixed.

independent.q: Stretch: is the recipe mainly humorous or mainly serious? Give one reason for each view
independent.a: Humorous: the playful recipe form; serious: the call for justice and respect. A balanced judgement.

exit.q: The extended metaphor in The British is a...
Answer the ponder in one sentence: what makes Britain's 'dish' work?
exit.a: For example: every ingredient matters and must be treated with justice.
